summary:
Nevada is one of the more protective US states for a trans visitor, though it sits below the most-protective tier. A July 2026 national legal risk assessment places Nevada in its Low-Risk group, crediting the state with fairly robust non-discrimination policies while finding it falls short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people.

State anti-discrimination law covers gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public accommodations under statutes effective 1 October 2011 and extended throughout state codes effective 1 July 2017. In November 2022 voters approved Question 1 by 58%, writing sexual orientation and gender identity or expression into the state Constitution's equal protection clause.

Nevada's hate-crime law adds penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived characteristics; gender identity or expression was added by a May 2013 amendment effective 1 October 2013, and a hate-crime reporting hotline opened in January 2025.

Identity documents are among Nevada's most permissive features. Since 2016 Nevada Vital Records issues a corrected-gender birth certificate on two affidavits alone, with no sex reassignment surgery required; the DMV makes similar changes to driver's licences and state IDs. The state offers an X third-gender designation on licences, birth certificates and state IDs with no medical documentation (2019). A 2017 law signed 22 June 2017 abolished the 1988 requirement that trans people publish their names in newspapers before legal sex changes.

Facilities access is not restricted by state law: the Movement Advancement Project's Equality Map, which tracks state-by-state rules on whether trans people may use public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, does not record a Nevada ban.

Care access has a mixed record. Health insurers are barred under state law from discriminating against transgender patients. The state Medicaid agency announced in March 2018 it would cover sex-reassignment surgery. A bill passed June 2023 and effective 1 January 2024 requires insurers, including Medicaid, to cover all medically necessary gender-affirming treatments. The governor vetoed the broader SB 302 omnibus in 2023, which would have shielded gender-affirming care and mandated Medicaid surgery coverage.

In May 2023 the governor signed legislation explicitly protecting transgender and intersex individuals in state correctional facilities, one of the areas the July 2026 assessment still flags as under-protective in practice.

School sport moved the other way. In April 2025 the Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association reversed its 2016 policy and now requires transgender athletes to compete under their sex assigned at birth. A governor-supported 2026 ballot initiative to generally determine school sports eligibility by sex assigned at birth failed to reach the November 2026 ballot.

Anti-bullying law SB 504, effective 1 July 2015, expressly lists gender identity or expression as a protected ground and directs school policies, reporting, parent notification and staff training. Conversion therapy on minors has been banned since 1 January 2018.
tangentialFactors:
Nevada's position is favourable relative to most of the United States: it sits in the Low-Risk group alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, directly below the most-protective tier. Several states in that same period moved sharply in the opposite direction, including Kansas's March 2026 law invalidating non-assigned-sex birth certificates and licences.

The April 2025 reversal by the Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association tracks a national pattern of school-sport eligibility rules being rewritten around sex assigned at birth, though Nevada's own 2026 ballot initiative on the same question did not qualify for the ballot.

The gap the July 2026 assessment identifies is in healthcare equity and incarcerated trans people rather than in general non-discrimination, so a visitor's exposure in everyday public settings is lower than in most states while institutional settings remain weaker.

State correctional facilities operate under a May 2023 statute explicitly protecting transgender and intersex inmates, although the July 2026 assessment still rates protections for incarcerated transgender people as falling short.

Residents can obtain a corrected-gender birth certificate on two affidavits without surgery, change the gender marker on a driver's licence or state ID on the same basis, and hold an X designation on all three documents with no medical documentation.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Nevada's protections for incarcerated transgender people are enforced in practice, as opposed to on paper, is not resolved by the sources; the July 2026 assessment flags the area as a shortfall without documenting specific Nevada incidents.

The healthcare-equity gap named in the July 2026 assessment is not broken down by measure, so which specific care-access failures it refers to in Nevada is unresolved.

Nevada's position on any given federal measure in force or in litigation should be checked before travel, since several federal orders have been blocked or enjoined in court.
